  • The Toronto-based tech company stated in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.
  • Recent findings suggest that the attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the firm’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Password manager maker 1Password has confirmed that some customer information was taken in a recent intrusion into its internal systems, but that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed.

The Toronto-based tech company stated in a blog post published Wednesday that it detected an intrusion on November 19, in which an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate account with GitHub, which the company uses to share and store its source code.

Recent findings suggest that the attacker used that employee’s access to push malicious code to the firm’s internal servers, which allowed the hacker to download some data about 1Password customers, including their names and the email address that they use for logging into their account. The company said that the attacker also took details about when a 1Password account was created and when a user last logged in.

It has been revealed that 1Password remarked that customer vaults, which store their passwords, were “at no point” available to the attacker. The company also said that it doesn’t have access to customer account passwords or their secret keys, which are used to scramble their passwords so that 1Password cannot see them.

In addition, the firm said that its apps and extensions are unaffected by the incident.

It’s unclear how the attacker gained access to the employee’s corporate account, and a spokesperson for 1Password did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.

Sources indicate that 1Password did not say whether it had notified customers whose information was taken in the breach, or how many customers had information taken. We’ve also asked if the organization has received any communication or demands from the hackers. We’ll revision if we hear back from 1Password.

It has been revealed that the company touts millions of customers and more than 200,000 businesses who use its password manager products to store their passwords, credentials, payment card information, and more. Security experts have long recommended password managers as a better way of generating stronger credentials and keeping track of online accounts.

    New York state bans AI chatbot toys for kids

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (487 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Companies violating the five year ban will face a $15,000 per day fine.
    • In a recent development, newly introduced York governor Kathy Hochul has signed into law a five-year ban on the sale of AI chatbot toys, including dolls and robots that use the internet to converse with children.
    • "Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk," Hochul said in a statement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Companies violating the five year ban will face a $15,000 per day fine.

    In a recent development, newly introduced York governor Kathy Hochul has signed into law a five-year ban on the sale of AI chatbot toys, including dolls and robots that use the internet to converse with children. The new law comes with some teeth, including steep daily fines for each violation enforced by the state's attorney general.

    "Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk," Hochul said in a statement. Calling herself New York's first "mom governor," Hochul said the new measure was "deeply personal.".

    It has been revealed that the governor's press release cited the US Public Interest Research Group Education Fund (PIRG), that tested chatbot toys marketed to children aged three to 12. Some of the toys talked about sexually explicit subjects and provided advice that could create a fire hazard in homes. The toys had few or zero parental controls and the longer the conversation, the more safety limits weakened. Some toys could even record a child's voice or scan their face.

    "AI chatbots in children's toys are exposing young people to inappropriate content and putting their mental health at risk," stated Upcoming York attorney general Letitia James.

    Sources indicate that violators face civil penalties up to $15,000 per day for each violation, according to the governor's office. James added that her branch would "not hesitate to enforce this law and other measures to stop AI systems from doing harm. We won't allow our children's health to become the collateral damage of substantial tech.".

    In a recent development, hochul and Upcoming York State legislators recently enacted another law called "AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors," prohibiting unsafe chatbot features for children under 18, with civil penalties of up to $25,000 per infraction. Hochul also signed an executive order this summer, issuing a one-year ban data centers using 50MW or more.

    Sources indicate that anti-AI measures were a politically popular during US midterm elections, as Americans voted to restrict the country's data center boom. Data centers were the subject of 45 ballot measures in 10 states and 39 measures were passed to restrict the facilities in some form.

    In a statement, Amazon said the products it sells must follow US laws. "We require all products sold by third-party sellers in our store to comply with applicable laws and regulations," Amazon told NBC News. "Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families. We support efforts across the industry and government to put appropriate guardrails in place as this technology develops." However, the retail giant sells some 12 million different toys in the US (as of 2023), so complying with the NY AI chatbot law could be a tall order.

    Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's music.
    • Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.
    • Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's music.

    Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.

    Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.

    Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".

    Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran remarked in a statement on Wednesday.

    Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off.

    He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement mentioned.

    Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates stated: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

    "His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.".

    They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.

    Le Bon remarked there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart".

    "Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the Latest Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later.".

    Watch: Andy Taylor tells the BBC about his cancer diagnosis in 2023.

    Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".

    Kemp stated Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix.".

    In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".

    US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".

    Belinda Carlisle noted she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You.

    Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".

    Taylor (second left) married his wife Tracey at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Los Angeles in 1982.

    Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together.".

    She mentioned he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".

    Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songs.

    The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.

    He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.

    The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.

    Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.

    Duran Duran bridged the sounds of pop, funk, disco, punk and new wave with a sound that remains indelibly tied to the 1980s.

    Duran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs.

    Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.

    They became so popular in the US that the press labeled them the leaders of a "second British invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.

    During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station.

    The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.

    "We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.

    "We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral.".

    He went on to play on Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.

    Taylor quit Duran Duran at the height of their fame in 1985, but rejoined the band several times in the 2000s and contributed to their most recent album, Danse Macabre.

    After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.

    In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public looks for a reunion.

    When the group took the stage, Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.

    Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.

    Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a true Wild Boy.

    The parental controls arrive after months of concerns around Grok, X’s deepfake machine.

    The parental controls arrive after months of concerns around Grok, X’s deepfake machine.

    Sources indicate that X is finally rolling out parental controls that allow parents and guardians to manage teens’ accounts on the platform. While teens will retain ownership of their own account, parents and guardians will be able to see how much time their child has spent on X, set daily limits, require approval for latest followers, and limit For You recommendations to accounts a teen already follows.

    Recent findings suggest that “Parents and guardians cannot read private messages, see searches or viewing history, post as their teen, or access the account,” explains the X safety team. “Every change is recorded and visible to the teen.” The controls will also allow parents and guardians to filter specific words, turn off sensitive media content, control who can send direct messages to a teen, and see which accounts a teen has chatted with without seeing the messages.

    Sources indicate that parents and guardians can manage up to five teen accounts, and a teen can only be linked to a single parent or guardian account at a time. A teen and parent / guardian will both have to agree before the controls start. “Supervision on X starts with a handshake and ends automatically when a teen becomes an adult,” claims Mridul Singhai, product engineering lead at X. “Parents get guardrails, not a window into their teen’s private life. Simple, transparent, and built to grow with families.”.

    The new parental controls come just days after Oregon and Virginia both sued SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes. The complaint in Virginia accuses X owner Elon Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and describes Grok’s weak safeguards as “not a failure but a feature.” Three teens also filed a lawsuit against xAI earlier this year, claiming that Grok generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM) when launching its “spicy mode” last year. Grok was also undressing women and minors earlier this year.

    X admits its platform isn’t “designed for or promoted to children,” and it already restricts teen accounts to a protected mode, where sensitive media is restricted and targeted advertising is blocked. These latest parental controls may well help teens avoid the very worst parts of X, just as the platform faces more scrutiny from states and regulators.

    #128394. Latest Update: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (862 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems.
    • “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote.
    • Recent findings suggest that the statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”.

    “We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman noted he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”.

    Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”.

    According to recent reports, “It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”.

    But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.

    Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.

    Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”.

    Industry observers note that still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The tech giant noted in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.

    In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”.

    “As we remarked publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.

    The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The glitch compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control.

    Recent findings suggest that still, Anthropic is by no means the only firm that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.

    In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently.

    Sources indicate that “Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every tech giant seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.”.

    • Elon Musk's Neuralink has received FDA permission to launch the first "pivotal" trial for its implantable LINK brain-computer interface, the manufacturer unveiled.
    • "We've received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US," Neuralink announced on X.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The study will evaluate the efficacity and safety of the manufacturer’s LINK device.

    Elon Musk's Neuralink has received FDA permission to launch the first "pivotal" trial for its implantable LINK brain-computer interface, the manufacturer unveiled. The study represents a more advanced step in the company's efforts to develop a brain implant that allows people with paralysis to control devices using their brain alone. It will be open to a limited number of patients with ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis), a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that damages nerve cells controlling voluntary muscle movement.

    "We've received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US," Neuralink announced on X. "This builds off of our work with 30+ participants with Neuralink to date.".

    Neuralink hit a milestone last year when the firm revealed that its first participant with ALS named Bradford Smith was able to communicate using brain signals alone. "Neuralink has given me freedom, hope, and faster communication. ... It has improved my life so much. I'm so happy to be involved in something big that will help many people," Smith said at the time.

    Sources indicate that we've received FDA approval to launch LINK, the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US. This builds off of our work with 30+ participants with Neuralink to date.

    Those with ALS may be eligible. To learn more:https://t.co/dWhb5N4GdR pic.twitter.com/Vor7iXXCBA.

    — Neuralink (@neuralink) November 25, 2026.

    The FDA authorization was granted on an experimental basis, but it's a key step forward for Neuralink's LINK brain-implant system. The study will evaluate the ability of patients to control digital devices through thought, "with a focus on functional outcomes that improve independence in daily life," Neuralink wrote. It will also assess the system's long-term safety and reliability.

    WIth Neuralink's latest system, the tech giant's N1 implant is surgically placed in the skull, then the company uses its R1 robot to insert flexible electrodes into the brain. Neural activity from the brain associated with movement is then interpreted by software, which translates signals into commands for controlling computers or digital devices. The technology is designed to help patients communicate with the outside world, with the eventual goal to let them operate devices without keyboards or other physical controls.

    Neuralink noted patients with ALS may be eligible for the LINK trial, but it didn't specify other requirements or the number of participants. It now has approval recruit participants, then conduct the study under an approved clinical protocol. If the technology proves to be safe, the trial may allow Neuralink to apply for more advanced trials and eventually release LINK onto the market.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.

    Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.

    The Fresh Mexico Corrections Department stated that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.

    She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.

    Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.

    The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an patch.

    According to recent reports, the Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said.

    "It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.

    All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.

    However the prison where she was being held, the Western Fresh Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are right now allowed.

    The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

    Waymo conquered city streets — why does it keep stumbling on freeways?

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Repeated construction-zone violations and a California DMV ban have forced the autonomous vehicle giant off the freeway for the second time this year.﻿.
    • Repeated construction-zone violations and a California DMV ban have forced the autonomous vehicle giant off the freeway for the second time this year.﻿.
    • Most people know not to try to pass highway patrol cars while performing a traffic break on a freeway.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Repeated construction-zone violations and a California DMV ban have forced the autonomous vehicle giant off the freeway for the second time this year.﻿.

    Repeated construction-zone violations and a California DMV ban have forced the autonomous vehicle giant off the freeway for the second time this year.﻿.

    Most people know not to try to pass highway patrol cars while performing a traffic break on a freeway. But on November 6th, a driverless Waymo on Interstate 280 failed that test.

    According to recent reports, video reveals the robotaxi attempting to overtake two California Highway Patrol cruisers during a traffic break, a moving violation that could get a human driver’s license suspended. For Waymo, it was the latest in a series of freeway blunders that eventually led to the California DMV last week banning its vehicles from all state interstates.

    Construction zones have also posed a challenge. Between October and November 2026, the manufacturer reported a total of 11 instances in which its vehicles failed to recognize that a freeway lane was closed because of construction and drove into the restricted area anyway, according to a recently filed recall.

    It has been revealed that with all these violations piling up, Waymo decided last week to pause commercial freeway rides across all of its US markets. It was a bruising setback for the global leader of autonomous driving, exposing how easily its multibillion-dollar technology can still be tripped up by basic road rules.

    According to recent reports, for years, the autonomous vehicle industry assumed freeways would be the easy part — no jaywalkers, no unprotected left turns — while dense cities were seen as the ultimate battle. Yet Waymo has flipped that script, racking up millions of urban miles while repeatedly stumbling on the interstate.

    It was a bruising setback for the global leader of autonomous driving, exposing how easily its multibillion-dollar technology can still be tripped up by basic road rules.

    In a recent development, this was neither the first time Waymo was forced to pause freeway operations nor the first time it had been caught blundering into construction sites. Earlier this year, the organization temporarily halted freeway rides after its robotaxis entered active construction zones in Arizona and California. It issued a recall in June and gradually resumed freeway operations starting in late July after updating its software.

    But experts note that the recall didn’t work, as evidenced by the subsequent violations.

    ”The most concerning part about this is now we have a pattern for Waymo: They issue a recall, it doesn’t fix the problem, but they keep scaling up anyway,” says Phil Koopman, emeritus professor in electrical and computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University and a researcher specializing in autonomous vehicle safety.

    In an interview, Koopman says Waymo is using recalls as “Band-Aids,” which he argues doesn’t really address the root of the problem. In addition to the freeway snafus, Waymo also filed a recall related to the intersection crash where its vehicle failed to detect a police officer directing traffic. In short, the car followed the officer’s orders until passing traffic blocked its view, at which point its software lost track of the “stop” command and drove into the intersection on its own, the manufacturer remarked in the recall report filed with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Waymo later updated its software across its entire fleet so the vehicles remember manual traffic signals even when an officer is temporarily blocked from view.

    Sources indicate that there have been other recalls related to Waymo passing stopped school buses and driving through flooded roadways. This has led Koopman to theorize that rather than solving the underlying perception and reasoning flaws, Waymo is using “dynamic geofencing” to route around known flood zones or using real-time GPS feeds of school buses until a car encounters an unmapped situation.

    “The most concerning part about this is now we have a pattern for Waymo: They issue a recall, it doesn’t fix the problem, but they keep scaling up anyway.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “It felt to me like they were really not being able to fix these problems,” he says. “They’re putting Band-Aids on and getting on with scaling.”.

    In response to the California DMV order, Waymo remarked it’s working closely with regulators on a solution, noting that its vehicles haven’t crashed or injured anyone while driving through restricted areas on the freeway.

    According to recent reports, “Our ridehailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week,” Waymo spokesperson Chris Pappas remarked last week. “We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”.

    Since its inception, Waymo has typically avoided highways, opting instead for longer routes that stick to local roads when ferrying passengers. This has not gone unnoticed by the firm’s customers, who often complain their trips can take longer because the vehicles are prohibited from using routes that travel on highways. But in late 2025, Waymo stated it was ready to hit the highway.

    “Freeway driving is one of those things that’s very easy to learn, but very hard to master when we’re talking about full autonomy without a human driver as a backup,” Dmitri Dolgov, co-CEO of Waymo, mentioned in a November 2025 briefing with reporters. “And at scale. So it took time to do it properly with a strong focus on system safety and reliability.”.

    “Freeway driving is one of those things that’s very easy to learn, but very hard to master.”.

    Recent findings suggest that now it seems as if Waymo may have jumped the gun. The tech giant’s decision to pull back from the freeway, twice in one year, reflects the enormous stakes of operating driverless vehicles at high speeds. At 10 to 25 mph on a city street, applying the brakes solves almost any confusion, and crash lethality is drastically lower. At 60 or 70 mph, stopping distances stretch out, and any mistake involving a roadside worker or stranded motorist is nearly 100 percent fatal. And if the vehicle gets confused and needs to ping a remote operator for assistance, the latency of that connection and the time it takes to receive a reply becomes a major liability.

    According to recent reports, koopman thinks that subtle edge cases — like a gap in construction cones or a cop’s hand gesture — are tripping Waymo up right after its transition to end-to-end machine learning. Unlike older modular systems where engineers could write explicit rules, statistical models struggle when familiar objects appear in unfamiliar contexts.

    “If you’ve trained on the individual elements, their combination presents a special meaning that is different than usual,” he states. “A stop sign folded out on a school bus is completely different from a stop sign on a post... Everything I’ve seen is consistent with the hypothesis that it’s having trouble with subtle contextual clues.”.

    According to recent reports, for Waymo, solving for the freeway is essential if the tech giant wants to continue expanding its service area to include popular ridehailing destinations, like airports. Waymo’s future reliability will depend on it. While safety engineers want to do the right thing, executives face massive market pressure to ship “good enough” fixes and apologize later, Koopman argues. And because traffic tickets and standard fines don’t deter well-capitalized tech giants like Alphabet, regulators need mandatory public transparency — not quiet software patches via recalls.

    Sources indicate that “If DMV gets a neutral look without political pressure, they’re going to say, ‘Fool me once, shame on you,’” Koopman says. “They can’t just accept Waymo saying, ‘Trust us, bro, we fixed it this time for sure.’”.

    #128387. From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3652 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    From minimalist to maximalist: Ars staffers show off their home offices

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working.
    • As Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices.
    • Recent findings suggest that as an apartment dweller in Fresh York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ars Technica is a place that has always leaned into remote working. Since its beginnings in 1998, Ars has never had a single, central office—a setup that makes for a great commute to work, with little risk of getting stuck in traffic.

    As Ars staffers step away from their desks for a few days to spend some time with family and friends, we wanted to give you a look inside our home offices. We’ve got all sorts of setups, tucked into basements, dens, spare bedrooms, apartment corners, and lofts. They run the gamut from minimalist “here’s my laptop and monitor” setups to “I really like collecting things.” Without any further ado, let’s dig in:.

    Recent findings suggest that as an apartment dweller in Fresh York City, I’ve usually set up my home work station in a small corner of my residence along with sometimes decamping for local cafes or coworking spaces. My current hodgepodge of equipment is probably on the minimal side compared to many members of the Ars team.

    I’m usually multitasking on my basic monitor display and work laptop configuration, with the monitor sitting on a stack of several books (apologies in particular to Mary Beard’s excellent history of the Roman Republic, titled SPQR).

    It has been revealed that accessories plugged into the work laptop include a simple Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse and a Logitech K380 keyboard that I’ve often brought along with me to public workspaces. Sometimes I’ll use the built-in Macbook Air keyboard, but I like having the laptop display elevated, whether I’m working at home or elsewhere.

    My personal Apple M4 Macbook Air usually sits on the side, where I primarily use my old, battered pair of Sennheiser HD 518 headphones to listen to music during the work day.

    Sources indicate that I have a simple standing desk, but it’s not the easiest to change positions, so I wouldn’t recommend it for anyone who wants to adjust frequently. Whenever I’m sitting, I sometimes switch between a simple wooden chair from Ikea and a more ergonomic chair.

    Aside from an assortment of coasters and a tea container turned pen holder, my desk also holds a painted dinosaur sculpture (courtesy of my young son) and two versions of the Spot It! Matching game (also for my son’s entertainment).

    Recent findings suggest that last but not least, I have a pair of Powerblock dumbbells tucked under my work desk. I wouldn’t say they feature heavily in my work day, but they’re easily accessible if I have 15-20 minutes to spare.

    Greetings from my basement hobbit hole! My desk sits across from a workbench area that was already here when we got the house. I have labeled drawers full of PC parts, tools, and cables accumulated over decades. The drawer organization was quite the upgrade over my previous solution of “chuck everything in unlabeled storage tubs.”.

    My current PC setup is an AceMagic W1 mini PC running Fedora, and a Blackview Intel N150 I keep on Windows for audio recording (PipeWire is fussy). The two are connected to my inputs and monitors via a KVM so I can switch back and forth at the press of a button.

    The monitors are mismatched thrift finds. One is an HP, the other Sansui. The TV is a similar story—an old Samsung LCD that set me back $10 at the thrift store. I use it as a third monitor for watching PC streams. An Onn Android box is also connected, though it rarely earns its keep.

    Sources indicate that below the TV sits a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, a repurposed B2B video-conference gadget modded to run LineageOS. It handles smart-home controls and tracks my solar production during the day. There’s also a Flashforge 5M printer in the corner, and the pegboard wall holds tools, Mega Man figures, and about 10 years’ worth of convention badges.

    The back closet is the scary part: old consoles, spare drives, boards, and parts for every project I’ll get to “eventually.” The chair is a Dowinx gaming chair I grabbed on a Slickdeals whim—it’s fine, but I wouldn’t recommend it to anyone.

    The rug-patterned Dude mousepad really ties the desk together, man.

    In a recent development, I’m something of an outlier at Ars, in that I use Windows most days. I’m no great lover of Windows 11, but I still use it thanks to years of computing inertia. My machine is custom, built in early 2024 with a Raptor Lake Core i7 (that thankfully did not fall victim to the overvolting bug) and an RTX 4070 Ti. It has long been my preference to build my own PC for gaming and work to ensure easier repairs and upgrades. Although with the prices of components being what they are, I hope all these parts last a very long time.

    The primary monitor on the bottom is an Alienware ultrawide OLED. I got it for gaming, but it’s also a nice productivity display that gives me lots of room to keep windows visible. Above that, I have an Asus ProArt LCD calibrated in sRGB for photography work. I’ll get to the keyboard, but I do want to point out my preferred mouse, a Logitech MX Vertical. I have carpal tunnel issues, and this thing has been a lifesaver.

    It has been revealed that I believe organizing my desk before taking the photo would be a form of lying, so rest assured this is what it looks like on an average day. I have a few organizers to keep phones and various accessories from getting scattered around my Uplift sit-stand desk (seen here in sitting mode), which I quite like. The chair is a Herman Miller Aeron, which I don’t like as much. It’s fine and has plenty of adjustments, but the mesh is very hard. You should only buy one on sale, and if you do, get a cushion.

    Sources indicate that above the desk are some Star Trek cross-stitches, courtesy of my talented wife. The dangling ’90s-era computer components are a mobile I put together many years ago, featuring a neat Intel i486 DEC socket board and some SDRAM.

    In a recent development, I’m not a particularly neat person. My natural state is to have two or three projects half-exploded all over every surface: piles of 3D-printed prototypes, spools of wire, a soldering iron, laser-cut acrylic for a pinball project, the packaging from something I recently opened and need to sort through. Those aren’t random examples; that’s the contents of my workbench behind me on the opposite wall of my office as I type this. It’s a bit of a mess.

    To combat that tendency, I make a concerted effort to keep the desk where I spend so many hours of the day calm and a place where I can focus. It doesn’t always last! But I’m always at least striving for it, and what I find helps is having a very intentional design where everything has a place.

    According to recent reports, my desk surface is made from rubberwood butcher block, on Flexispot motorized legs. I recently picked up another rubberwood slab to build the cantilevered shelf. The supports neatly tuck away my M1 Max Mac Studio, which is still a great little workhorse with 64 gigs of RAM, and my Arturia audio interface, which I use to record line-in sources like synthesizers.

    On the left is a task lamp and a pen holder with six discrete holes. This fits in with the intentional design part: I have to pick the six things I want handy, and I can’t just pack it with more and more stuff. Right now that’s my Apple Pencil, a Pentel mechanical pencil, an Olfa mini snap-off blade knife, and a selection of three Pigma Micron pens in different line widths.

    Recent findings suggest that the right side holds an Aiyima 10th anniversary hi-fi stack: A20 amp, D20 DAC, and T20 pre-amplifier. The speakers are SVS Ultra Evolution Nanos. They’re sitting on the latest version of some 3D-printed stands I’ve been designing. I print them with hollow legs and then fill them with concrete for mass and stability.

    Recent findings suggest that since I know Ryan is going to flex on everyone with his keyboard collection, I have to try my best to keep up with my daily driver. It’s a Percent Canoe v2 case, running Holy Panda switches modified with 63 gram SPRiT springs for a slightly lighter touch, and GMK Bento keycaps. This was a pandemic build project, and it has served me well since.

    In a recent development, I used to run multiple monitors, but I’ve found that I don’t focus as well with them and prefer a singular spot to pay attention to. I’m using an Apple Studio Display because I’m very picky about pixel density. I opted to order it without the stand so I can run it on an ergo arm.

    Sources indicate that when I built the shelf for my desk, I fabricated a mounting bracket for the arm out of schedule 40 steel pipe and a 3D-printed sleeve that sits in a pocket CNC’d out. Since it sits flush on the underside, I don’t have to use a clamp that would extend down into the space where I keep my Mac and audio interface.

    Industry observers note that when I need a secondary display, or I want to use my Apple Pencil in Photoshop or Illustrator, I use an iPad Pro. I used to have a dedicated Wacom monitor, but I find this much more convenient both in terms of space efficiency and ergonomics. If I’m not really leaning into hand drawing or lettering, I do most of my graphic work with a mouse, which is at the moment a Logitech MX Master 3S.

    To wrap up the final items, the chair is an Aeron I bought new in 2003. I’ve had to repair it a few times over the years, but it’s either been things I consider wear items (wheels, armrests, gas cylinder) or Herman Miller has replaced under warranty. It was a big purchase for me at the time, but it’s ended up being a great investment. That’s Sophie draped over it, one of our four cats.

    Tucked next to my desk, behind the subwoofer under the little side table, is my home server and networking gear. The server runs Unraid and is primarily used for my Jellyfin media collection and Home Assistant. Networking is a combination of Unifi and Eero, but at some point I’d like to ditch the Amazon gear and go fully native Unifi.

    Sources indicate that I spend a lot of time in my office. It’s not just a place to edit, write, and do other Ars-y things. It’s also my rehearsal space and a place to relax and unwind when I need some me-time. Long-time readers won’t be surprised to see Apple hardware front and center. I’ve been using Macs since college, and they’ve done alright by me ever since. My daily driver is a first-gen Mac Studio (M1 Max) with 64GB of RAM, which drives two Apple Studio Displays. As a long-time mouse hater, I use a Magic Trackpad along with my extended Apple keyboard. Underneath the desk is a UPS and a Thunderbolt disk enclosure that is one of my two backups.

    The bookshelves are where my home networking gear lives. That includes a Synology DS920+ that backs up all of the computers in the house, serves up media, and runs my instance of Mealie. The Eero 6+ handles home networking, with everything in my office except my MacBook Pro connected via Ethernet. As much as I’d like to live a paperless existence, the HP printer-scanner-copier combo still gets some use. They’re difficult to see, but to the right of the G4 Cube (sadly inoperable) on top of the bookshelf sit an Apple TV and M2 Mac mini, which hook up to the 43-inch TV. My graphite iBook and eMate are now resigned to propping up bibs from races and other cycling events.

    Industry observers note that this is my office, which is the place where I am much of the time. The chair is a Herman Miller Embody and is one of the best things I’ve ever spent money on. The desk is a standy desk that I don’t stand at nearly often enough; the work PC is a Mac Studio; and the gaming PC is a frankenbox with a cockpit running Windows 10 LTSC (from my cold dead hands, etc., etc.). The Linux boxen are headless and are mostly banished to the closet.

    According to recent reports, the paintings (including the awesome Apollo 12 SCE-to-aux one) are all originals by the inimitable Stephen Quick, who does a hell of a job with commissions. What started as a funny idea about a Warhol-esque take on the many faces of Kurt Russel kinda turned over a couple of years into somewhat of a “these are some actors whose work I like” series. My buddies and I went to a lot of movies when we were teenagers, so the imagery sparks good memories for me.

    Sources indicate that the rest of the office has space stuff in it, especially the part behind where I was standing to do the pano sot. I’ve heard it remarked that when a man hits his 40s, he must choose between becoming obsessed with World War 2 history or smoking meats; I did kind of a variation on “World War 2” and fell deeply into historic human spaceflight. Apollo is kind of my jam, and some weekends you can even catch me docenting at Space Center Houston’s Saturn V exhibit! (Yeah, it’s maybe not as pretty as the exhibits at Marshall or KSC, but the JSC Saturn V is the only one made of flight stages end to end!).

    Welcome to the mess of wires, monitors, and handheld fidgets that is my loft desk. Let’s take a quick tour along with the rest of my gaming cave/mid-life crisis Mario collection that lives right by it.

    It has been revealed that my office setup is probably a lot simpler—basic?—than most of my Ars colleagues. I use an adjustable wood-top desk that allows me to stand or sit while I work. I do almost all of my writing and editing on a MacBook Air, and I have a spare available in case I need it. Sometimes I travel with both MacBooks so I can use one for writing and the other for monitoring a rocket launch, press conference, or other event. I also work a lot from my porch, where I can enjoy the fresh air and quiet mornings on our ranch in rural Texas.

    An iMac and a second monitor stand behind the laptops. I generally use them to watch conferences, rocket launch livestreams, weather radar, or live news. It just depends on what’s happening any given day. One of the things I love about the space beat is there’s something happening nearly every day, and it’s possible to cover much of it from home. There are often multiple things happening the same day, so the dual-screen setup becomes especially handy then. For example, I can use one monitor to watch what SpaceX is doing at Starbase, Texas, and another to watch a rocket launch in Florida. I use a ring light behind my desk for TV interviews or podcast appearances.

    Sources indicate that absent from my desk is my large collection of space swag stowed away in storage boxes. Perhaps I will bring it out to add to my workspace for a future Ars Staff Source. For now, I use a mouse pad from the European Space Agency that I’ve had for at least 15 years. The mouse pad features ESA’s astronomy missions that were in development or operations at the time. All of the missions have now released, and some have long been decommissioned. It’s a good reminder of how long it takes to design, develop, build, and launch science missions. Anyone who claims this stuff is easy is being dishonest.

    It has been revealed that this image is a bit misleading, in that it implies I work on the pictured PC (RTX 4070, Ryzen 5 3600X, 32GB RAM) and sit at my desk while doing so. That’s occasionally true, but more often, I can be found wandering around my apartment with my M4 MacBook Air during work hours. I don’t even sit at my desk to game much anymore—on the off chance that I’m playing a game the Steam Deck can’t handle natively, I’ll stream it from my PC to my Steam Deck using Moonlight and Apollo (previously Moonlight and Sunshine).

    Recent findings suggest that you may also notice that my desk, from a organization called Uplift, is adjustable. As it turns out, I don’t enjoy standing while working, so the ability to loft my tabletop skyward has been chiefly deployed in the service of making it easier to retrieve something I’ve dropped down there.

    In a recent development, at night, my desk often moonlights as a craft area; I swap out my keyboard (a Wobkey Rainy75) for a cutting mat, and I’m ready to build some Gundam, assemble a book nook, or tackle a crochet pattern (a few amigurumi are scattered around my desk to keep me company). You can see some of my supplies on the left, but I have other stuff stashed in drawers and various containers that I can bring to my desk as needed.

    So sure, I do work here sometimes.

    My wife Anna and I rent an apartment in Chicago, and we’ve chosen the city life over, well, space. As such, my 10-by-10-foot office space serves multiple functions. I use it primarily for work, but since Anna and I are both big gamers and she is often camped out with the PlayStation 5 in the living room, I have my own gaming setup in the office. It’s cramped, but it works!

    According to recent reports, I do editing, news hits, and most other work during the day, but I’m a night owl at heart and find that I can only do heavy writing—like on longer feature articles—at night, so I’m picturing both the daytime and nighttime view here. I have a collection of Govee lights (Govee Hexa panels, several RGB Edison bulbs, and a Star Light Aurora galaxy projector) to max out the vibes for those nighttime focus (and gaming) sessions.

    We moved into this place in the dead of the pandemic, and I bought most of the stuff in this office during that year or shortly afterward, so it’s a very 2020–2021-coded array of hardware.

    It has been revealed that the desk is a Secretlab Magnus Pro, and the chair is a Steelcase Gesture. I love the desk, but I have mixed feelings about the chair. I don’t like the material of the Herman Miller Aeron, but people kept telling me to buy an ergonomic chair for long-term back health, so I bought the other one everyone recommends. To be frank, I’m never fully comfortable in it, though, and wish I had just said “life is short” and bought something comfy and bad for me!

    The main machine is a 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M1 Max, 64GB of RAM, and a 2TB hard drive—still holding strong after five years. I also have an Alienware Aurora R10—hear me out—prebuilt gaming desktop with a Ryzen 9 5900X and an RTX 3080. When I bought it, it was during the COVID-times GPU shortage, and there was absolutely no other way to get the GPU I wanted. The system is loud, hot, and hard to work with; I want very much to replace it with something custom, but the need has not yet arisen. I tend to hold on to stuff until it literally stops working.

    In a recent development, as for monitors, the center monitor is a 27-inch, 1440p, 240 Hz OLED Asus XG27AQDMGZ. The left and right monitors are both 27-inch 4K, 60 Hz IPS Dell U2720Qs. I’ve got a pair of Audioengine A2+ speakers, plus a Blue Yeti X, a Logitech Lighta Glow, and the good ol’ Logitech C920 for video and voice calls.

    According to recent reports, then there’s input: a Keychron K1 Pro keyboard, a Razer Orochi V2 mouse, and a Sony DualSense controller. I’ve got a Belkin charging station for my iPhone 17 Pro, AirPods Pro, and Apple Watch Series 7, plus AirPods Max on a headphone hanger on the front of the desk. The CalDigit E5 Thunderbolt hub is doing a lot of work here!

    I feel fortunate to have a job that allows me to occasionally apply my lifelong love affair with video games. My favorite game of all time is The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim (Morrowind is a close second), and I like Bethesda games in general. I’ve got a working (but mostly useless) Fallout Pip-Boy, which ought to count for something! I also have a few other Skyrim knickknacks hanging about. And if you’re a Star Trek: The Next Generation viewer, you might have already noticed the desk mat.

    I do enjoy playing games at my desk sometimes, but after I sit at the computer all day, I often want to be somewhere else when winding down. So pictured here is the other half of the room. The leather armchair I use for console gaming is paired with a leather ottoman (the colors don’t match because, again, COVID-era supply limitations).

    I have an LG C1 OLED TV with a PlayStation 5 Pro, a PlayStation 3 that is backward-compatible with PlayStation 1 and 2 games, a Nintendo Switch I barely touch, and three Analogue FPGA retro consoles: the Super Nt, Mega Sg, and 3D.

    It’s a tiny room to spend so much time in, but after almost seven years in this apartment, it certainly feels like home!

    Industry News: The canceled Tesla Cybertruck is the fastest-selling used truck in America

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it introduced.
    • In a recent development, the automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model.
    • According to iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that tesla Cybertruck sales never reached the lofty heights CEO Elon Musk predicted when it introduced. But the futuristic, steel-clad EV is finding latest life in the used car market, according to analysis of sales figures by iSeeCars.com.

    In a recent development, the automotive search engine and research platform analyzed more than 1.1 million sales of one- to five-year-old used vehicles in October 2026 and measured the average days on market by drivetrain, vehicle type, and individual model. The upshot: The Tesla Cybertruck was the fastest-selling used truck, averaging just 39.1 days on the market compared with 65.5 days for trucks overall. Used Cybertrucks sold faster than any other truck, including the Ford Maverick Hybrid, which held the No. 2 spot, and the Rivian R1T, in third place.

    According to iSeeCars.com, the Cybertruck’s sales performance lines up with a broader pattern in the used vehicle market: Used battery electric vehicles are hot sellers right now, with 16 of the 25 fastest-selling used cars fully electric. EVs are even edging out hybrids in terms of average days on market. EVs average 45.6 days on market compared to 54.5 days for hybrids and 61 days for gasoline-powered vehicles. Not every EV is selling well, however. For instance, iSeeCars.com found that the Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-selling vehicle in the study, averaging 134.3 days on the market, more than twice the overall industry average.

    Sources indicate that karl Brauer, executive analyst at iSeeCars.com, told TechCrunch that high gasoline prices have changed consumer-buying habits, prompting more people to opt for an EV or hybrid over an internal combustion engine vehicle. If high prices persist, as they have since March, that trend could continue.

    Keep in mind that these were October sales, the month before Musk confirmed Tesla would stop making the Cybertruck in 2027. Fuel prices and the relative rarity of Cybertrucks in the used car market were driving demand even before the cancellation announcement, Brauer mentioned.

    “The Cybertruck has only been out for a few years, so you have a lot of used ones coming off lease and entering the used car market for the first time,” he said, adding that used Cybertrucks are cheap relative to their MSRP.

    The impending cancellation will likely fuel used Cybertruck sales, although the pace may ebb and flow over the next year.

    “The canceling of the new Cybertruck is making people kind of aware — it’s like, oh wow, these things aren’t going to be coming anymore,” Brauer remarked. “Whatever demand is for them, supply will not be continuing to grow.”.

    Brauer stated that once production of the Cybertruck ends — which is expected in summer 2027 — sales of used versions may pop once again.

    “When the last one is being produced, that’ll probably reignite things again, and for a few months after that,” he mentioned.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Any responsible adult should probably check on their teen's X usage.

    It has been revealed that elon Musk's X has finally introduced parental controls for kids aged 13 to 17, allowing parents and guardians to manage their teen's experience on the platform. Teens' accounts will now default to protected mode, with sensitive media restricted and targeted advertising blocked. The fresh settings will also give families "additional tools on top of those defaults," the platform announced.

    According to recent reports, those extra tools let adults in charge of teens see how much time their kids have spent on X and set a daily limit, require approval for upcoming followers, and limit For You recommendations to accounts the teen already follows. They can also filter specific words, turn off sensitive media content, allow parents to control who can send direct messages, and see which accounts their teen has chatted with one-on-one (without seeing the messages themselves).

    Recent findings suggest that to use the upcoming parental controls, follow the guide in X's help center. "Linking starts with the parent or guardian and finishes with the teen. Both consumers have to agree," the platform states.

    Industry observers note that X emphasized that the new controls let parents manage content without prying into their kids' lives. "Parents and guardians cannot read private messages, see searches or viewing history, post as their teen, or access the account," the manufacturer wrote. Parents will be able to control up to five teens' accounts.

    There are reasons that parents should probably keep teens far away from X. In the last five years, it's been rife with complications including hate speech, AI-generated CSAM, misinformation, deepfake images, a lack of moderation, unauthorized AI training, propaganda, algorithms that amplify partisan content, AI bots, human trolls, and the omnipresence of awesome role model Elon Musk.

    Even X admits that it's not aimed at kids or teens. "While X is not designed for or promoted to children, and consumers must be at least 13 or older where required by law, we take extra care with the young people who are here," the company wrote. While claiming that "child safety is a top priority at X," the platform likely introduced the new rules to comply with current or future regulations in multiple states and countries.

    Latest Update: Hope for millions as cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Lenacapavir has received WHO's approval for HIV prevention.
    • Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.
    • The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has mentioned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lenacapavir has received WHO's approval for HIV prevention.

    Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.

    The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has mentioned.

    The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (Â£30) per person annually.

    Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.

    The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.

    The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.

    Focus on Africa podcast: Lenacapavir offering newly introduced hope for HIV prevention?

    Landmark deal paves way for cheaper HIV protection jab.

    Lenacapavir works by targeting the protective protein shell of HIV, disrupting the virus's ability to multiply and establish an infection in the body.

    In a landmark clinical trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa in 2024, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV.

    Health experts say the injection offers a major advantage over existing HIV prevention pills, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which must be taken every day and can carry social stigma.

    The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the drug for HIV prevention in July 2025.

    The Global Fund described the arrival of the drug in Africa as a "major breakthrough" in the fight against HIV, saying cheaper supplies would help reach millions more people at risk of infection.

    "These deliveries mark an unprecedented acceleration and expansion in access to a highly effective, quality-assured generic HIV prevention medicine in low- and middle-income settings," the group said in a statement on Wednesday.

    More than 189,000 people across 10 countries have already received their first injection of lenacapavir, according to the Global Fund.

    The organisation expects 24 countries to have received supplies by the end of this year and, working with the US government, aims to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.

    It is eventually expected to be available in 120 low- and middle-income countries.

    Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV globally, with adolescent girls and young women disproportionately affected.

    South Africa has the world's largest HIV-positive population, with nearly eight million people living with the virus. It is among the countries expected to receive the cheaper injection.

    Some 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV last year, while 570,000 died from HIV-related illnesses, according to the WHO.

    The rollout comes amid concerns that sweeping cuts to US foreign aid under President Donald Trump's administration could undermine decades of progress in tackling HIV in Africa, where many countries rely heavily on international funding for prevention and treatment.

    The UN aims to end Aids as a public health threat by 2030.

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1126 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

    Is authoritarian Vietnam ready to phase out the death penalty?

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Vietnam, a country once considered one of the world's most prolific executioners, is steadily reducing the number of crimes punishable by death.
    • On November 20, the country's National Assembly approved a revised Penal Code that abolishes capital punishment for six offenses, including drug trafficking, rape of a person under the age of 16 and crimes against humanity.
    • When the legislation takes effect next March, just four offences — treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production — will remain punishable by death, down from 44 in 1997.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Vietnam, a country once considered one of the world's most prolific executioners, is steadily reducing the number of crimes punishable by death.

    On November 20, the country's National Assembly approved a revised Penal Code that abolishes capital punishment for six offenses, including drug trafficking, rape of a person under the age of 16 and crimes against humanity.

    When the legislation takes effect next March, just four offences — treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production — will remain punishable by death, down from 44 in 1997.

    Although Hanoi has given little indication that it intends to do away with capital punishment entirely, few countries that still regularly execute prisoners have narrowed its legal application so considerably.

    The reforms are particularly striking given that they come as Vietnam's ruling Communist Party has intensified its crackdown on political dissent and independent civil society.

    Minister of Public Security General Luong Tam Quang said the changes reflect humanitarian considerations, the need for more proportionate sentencing and Vietnam's international integration, while maintaining a tough approach to crime, according to the state-run Vietnam News Agency.

    Vietnam's gradual reduction in the number of offenses punishable by death reflects an evolution in its criminal justice philosophy, said Tran Dai Lam, a lawyer at the ANVI law firm in Hanoi.

    "There is a growing recognition that the effectiveness of criminal law depends not necessarily on the severity of punishment, but on the certainty that criminal offenses are detected, prosecuted and punished," he told DW.

    Vietnam's latest reforms come barely a year after the National Assembly abolished the death penalty for eight other offenses, including embezzlement, bribery, espionage and the illegal transportation of drugs.

    The removal of capital punishment for drug trafficking is particularly significant given the prominence of narcotics-related offenses in Vietnam's criminal justice system and the country's proximity to the Golden Triangle, one of the world's largest illicit drug-producing regions.

    The upcoming legislation also provides for existing death sentences to be commuted to life imprisonment for offenses that will no longer carry the death penalty.

    Hai Luong, a lecturer in criminology at Griffith University in Australia, told DW that Vietnam has been taking a "retentionist-but-reductionist" approach.

    "Vietnam is reforming the death penalty rather than abolishing it," he noted. "The trend is towards a more limited and selective use of capital punishment, but not yet towards its complete removal.".

    According to Luong, the gradual reduction in capital offenses reflects Hanoi's efforts to modernize its legal system without relinquishing its authority to severely punish what it considers the most serious crimes.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Growing international recognition that capital punishment has little additional deterrent effect is also informing Vietnam's approach, he explained.

    Decades of harsh penalties for drug-related offenses have done little to stem the international narcotics trade, while the continued expansion of drug trafficking networks in Southeast Asia has raised questions about the effectiveness of executions as a crime prevention measure.

    Vietnam's growing integration into the international community, including its participation in international drug control conventions and closer diplomatic ties with Western countries, has also given Hanoi greater incentives to align its criminal justice system with international standards, Luong added.

    Vietnam's gradual retreat from capital punishment could also bring it closer to the European Union on human rights.

    Brussels has repeatedly called on Hanoi to abolish capital punishment, a subject regularly raised during bilateral human rights discussions.

    The EU, one of the world's most vocal advocates of abolition, has long opposed capital punishment as part of its foreign policy.

    An EU spokesperson told DW that Brussels welcomes "Vietnam's latest reduction in crimes punishable by capital punishment. This is a positive step and shows a disposition to consider gradual reform, leading towards a moratorium first and finally to the abolition of the death penalty.".

    "Any concrete step towards this ultimate goal would be very much welcomed by the EU," they added.

    However, Vietnam's reforms still fall short of international human rights standards, particularly since the death penalty remains available for drug-related offenses that do not involve intentional killing.

    Nor is there much evidence that progress on capital punishment is accompanied by improvements in other areas of Vietnam's human rights record, notably freedom of expression and association.

    It is also difficult to establish whether Vietnam's legislative reforms have resulted in fewer executions.

    In a recent development, the authorities classify execution statistics as state secrets. Amnesty International believes Vietnam continues to make extensive use of capital punishment, but it cannot provide reliable annual figures.

    Vietnam's capital punishment reform allows the state to continue executing people to fulfil its political and public security goals, "while also managing, or massaging, its international reputation through highly publicized 'reductionist' reforms," Daniel Pascoe, an associate professor of law at the City University of Hong Kong and an expert on capital punishment, told DW.

    For example, he added, although the recent abolition of the death penalty for drug trafficking is welcome, "it doesn't tell us whether the Vietnamese authorities will now simply charge a higher number of suspects with the drug production offense, which remains death-eligible.".

    Vietnam's reforms are part of a broader, if uneven, shift away from capital punishment in Southeast Asia.

    Cambodia, the Philippines and Timor-Leste have abolished the death penalty altogether. Malaysia abolished mandatory death sentences in 2023, while Indonesia's new Penal Code, which took effect this year, allows for death sentences to be commuted under certain conditions following a 10-year probationary period.

    However, Singapore has increased its use of capital punishment in recent years, particularly for drug-related offenses, while Myanmar's military authorities resumed executions in 2022 after a hiatus of more than three decades.

    Pascoe told DW that although the impact of Vietnam's reforms on execution numbers remains unclear, there is symbolic significance in one of Southeast Asia's most authoritarian governments visibly restricting the death penalty.

    "If a one-party state like Vietnam can reduce the scope of capital punishment, why shouldn't Singapore,Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Laos, Brunei and Myanmar also do so?" Pascoe added.

    The number of countries actively executing people is close to being at an all-time low, but those that are actively executing, such as Iran and Singapore, seem to be increasing their use, Sara Kowal, co-director of Eleos Justice, a research and advocacy initiative against the death penalty at Australia's Monash University, told DW.

    "Vietnam's dramatic reduction of death-eligible offences is another really positive sign that the global trend towards abolishing the death penalty is continuing,” Kowal stated.

    "It would be great to see Vietnam take the next step to establish an official moratorium on all executions," she added.

    According to Amnesty International, 17 countries carried out executions in 2025, among them China, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the US.

    #128374. SpaceX gets FCC approval to deploy 1 million satellites for its AI orbital data center

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (390 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    SpaceX gets FCC approval to deploy 1 million satellites for its AI orbital data center

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (390 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The FCC expects the initiative, called Starmind, to deploy it first satellite by November 2033.
    • The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has approved SpaceX's request to deploy 1 million satellites to build its AI orbital data center.
    • But can space-based data centers for AI really work?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The FCC expects the initiative, called Starmind, to deploy it first satellite by November 2033.

    The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has approved SpaceX's request to deploy 1 million satellites to build its AI orbital data center. SpaceX filed its application at the beginning of the year, presenting the initiative called Starmind as the better alternative for ground-based data centers. In its filing, the firm argued that "orbital data centers are the most efficient way to meet the accelerating demand for AI computing power," since they use "solar power with little operating and maintenance costs.".

    But can space-based data centers for AI really work? Critics doubt they can. Adam Becker, an astrophysicist and a critic of Elon Musk's space and AI ambitions, told AP that "it's not going to happen. The idea behind sending AI data centers outside our planet is so that they don't consume resources their ground-based counterparts do, like energy and water for cooling.

    However, critics of the proposal argue that space is a vacuum that traps heat inside objects and doesn't make cooling down hardware easier. In space, heat has to leave the satellites via radiation, and Becker explained that there are "basic physical limits" to radiating the heat out for all of them. In addition, that many satellites could cause in-orbit collisions and generate a huge amount of space junk.

    Recent findings suggest that FCC Chairman Brendan Carr believes that with this approval, though, America is "leading the world into the era of super intelligence." It opens a "bold fresh frontier," he added. Under the terms the FCC has approved, SpaceX has permission to deploy satellites into orbital layers spanning 50 kilometers, at altitudes between 500 meters and 1,002 kilometers.

    The company is required to deploy at lease one authorized satellite and place it into its assigned orbit by November 25, 2033. By the same date in 2035, it must have already deployed 100,000 satellites to their respective orbits. Three years later, on November 25, 2028, it must have already deployed 500,000 of the authorized satellites. All 1 million satellites must have already been placed in their assigned orbits no later than November 25, 2040. Musk previously said that SpaceX will start launching the satellites in 2027, but we'll have to wait and see if the company can stick to that timeline.
