    Breaking: Samsung’s R95H TV shows what RGB LED is capable of

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The excellent matte screen and ability to display a vast amount of colors makes the R95H one of the top RGB LED TVs available.﻿.
    • Sources indicate that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
    • If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The excellent matte screen and ability to display a vast amount of colors makes the R95H one of the top RGB LED TVs available.﻿.

    Sources indicate that if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

    If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

    Sources indicate that RGB LED TVs finally became affordable in 2026, and there’s always a lot of promise when newly introduced TV technologies come out. More color, higher brightness, improved performance — RGB LED TVs have a lot to prove. The Samsung R95H does a lot to deliver some of those promises. It can display more colors than other TVs I’ve seen so far this year, and the combination of light output and its matte screen makes it great for a bright room. RGB LED TVs might still be in their infancy, but the R95H is a solid TV that shows off the benefits of the new backlight tech.

    Recent findings suggest that because RGB LED TVs use individual red, green, and blue LEDs for their backlight (instead of a field of white or blue LEDs), they can deliver more colors than LED TVs. The Samsung R95H is one of the best examples of this in RGB LED TVs. It can fully display all the colors used in the vast majority of movies (which use the P3 color space) as well as the few that use the wider BT.2020 color space.

    Matte screen handles reflections incredibly wellGood color accuracy in Filmmaker mode.

    Some color crosstalk in white textGrayscale leans a bit cyanNo Dolby Vision support.

    In a recent development, the accuracy of those colors is also really good in HDR (it’s not quite as good in SDR, because the TV overbrightens most of them). Some earlier reviews called out mediocre color accuracy on the R95H, which I experienced with the first sample Samsung provided me in June. Samsung replaced that sample because I was worried something was wrong with it. But in Filmmaker mode with firmware version 1247 on my current 65-inch TV, I was pleasantly surprised by the R95H.

    HDR formats: HDR10 Plus, HDR10, HLG.

    HDMI inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 (one with eARC), up to 8 with Wireless One Connect box (sold separately).

    Audio support: Dolby Atmos, Dolby Digital, Auracast, Q-Symphony.

    Gaming features: VRR (up to 165Hz), ALLM, Game Bar, FreeSync Premium Pro.

    Sizes available (inches): 65, 75, 85.

    Colors are wonderfully lifelike. The green of the jungles in Planet Earth II, which uses the expanded BT.2020 color gamut, is beautifully vibrant, as are the hummingbirds that populate the trees. With movies that use P3, the foliage in the demo material on the Spears & Munsil Ultra HD Benchmark disc doesn’t have quite the same brilliance, but it still looks accurate and lifelike. Skin tones are natural. White and gray tones, like those in snow scenes, have a slight blue tint. It’s pretty minor, though.

    The R95H also has a good amount of light output — a full-field white screen measured 694 nits, while specular highlights hit 2,206 nits in Filmmaker mode (the TV’s most accurate picture mode). That’s similar to the Sony Bravia 7 II but short of the Bravia 9 II by a few hundred nits, and well short of the TCL X11L. Flagship 2026 OLEDs also have brighter highlights but dimmer full white screens, as is expected from OLED panels. Black levels on the R95H are really good for an LED display. There’s a bit of blooming, but not as excessive as I’ve seen on some RGB LED TVs this year. Overall, the Samsung R95H delivers an impactful image.

    The matte glare-free finish on the screen limits reflections well. I was never distracted by seeing the ceiling lights reflecting, as I can be with glossy screens. The black-level raise glitch — where ambient light gets caught behind the matte coating, causing the screen to look more gray than black — is much better. With a bright room, the black level rises a small amount, but it’s not washed out, and dark images still have depth.

    I had a great time gaming on it, too. Some earlier reviews noted challenges with smearing, but recent firmware seems to have addressed this for the most part. While racing in F1 24 in 120Hz mode, motion was smooth. The TV struggled a bit more when I set the Xbox to 60Hz, but I still enjoyed playing.

    Recent findings suggest that one inherent issue with RGB LED TVs, though, is color crosstalk — I’ve seen it to some extent on every RGB LED TV, though it’s least apparent on the Sony Bravia 9 II. It can happen when there’s a dominant color onscreen near a lighter color, such as white text, lighter skin tones, or white clouds. The dominant color can bleed into those lighter colors, influencing their tint. This happens a bit on the Samsung R95H. It’s most noticeable with white text. I saw it with news tickers on a red background, making the text look subtly pink, and with gaming, particularly while playing No Man’s Sky. Text displayed above a large yellow hologram has a slight yellow coloration that disappears if I move my view away from the hologram. In fleeting moments, it’s not too distracting, but when the color around the text is consistent, the effect is noticeable.

    Some TVs avoid this by defaulting the backlight to white and relying on the color filter, as LED TVs have for years. While doing that gets rid of any possibility of color crosstalk, it also diminishes the TV’s color brightness and wider gamut. So with RGB LED TV technology where it currently is in its development cycle, there’s going to be a tradeoff between some color crosstalk or a more limited color gamut.

    The R95H still has the same limitations as all Samsung TVs. There’s no Dolby Vision support (Samsung is an original backer of HDR10 Plus and will likely never support competitor Dolby Vision). It also runs on Tizen OS, which is continually one of my least favorite interfaces. Everything is buried a click or two deeper than it should be, including input selection, which makes it cumbersome to use. The remote, rechargeable via both USB-C and the solar panels on the back, is small, and I’m not a fan of the button layout — they’re bunched together, and the volume control feels clunky to me.

    The R95H is also still more expensive than most of its competitors. The Sony Bravia 9 II has better processing and is brighter, although it also has more blooming than the R95H. If you can fit a 75-inch in your space, the TCL X11L is significantly cheaper since it launched. I think it’s a better overall TV. Then there are the flagship OLEDs — Samsung’s S95H and the LG G6 — which are both less than or the same price as the R95H, depending on size. And OLED is still a step ahead of RGB LED in overall picture quality because of its better contrast.

    There’s still room for RGB LED TVs to improve. With its wide color gamut coverage, good out-of-the-box accuracy, and excellent matte screen, the Samsung R95H is one of the better ones to come out this year. Put up against those RGB competitors, it makes a strong case. But OLEDs are still better overall performers with superior contrast, and even cheaper non-RGB LEDs can get you most of the way there for less.

    Photography by John Higgins / The Verge.

    I set up each TV in my living room on my home theater credenza. I stream movies and reveals through the TV’s apps and from an Apple TV 4K, play discs on my Oppo UDP-203 4K Blu-ray player (including the Spears & Munsil Ultra HD Benchmark disc), and play games on my Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5. This is done at different times of the day and under different lighting conditions, with curtains open, with lamps and overhead lights on, or with blackout curtains up to keep the room dark. While I am a certified ISF Level 3 calibrator, I do not calibrate the TVs before measurement, as the overwhelming majority of TV owners don’t bother. So it’s vital to know how well the TVs perform out of the box, with minor tweaks in the menu anyone can do.

    For measurement, I use Portrait Displays’ Calman color calibration software, a Murideo 8K Seven pattern generator, an X-rite i1 Pro 3 spectrophotometer, Portrait Displays’ C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a Konica Minolta LS-100 luminance meter, and Leo Bodnar 4K lag tester.

    #128370. Industry News: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (686 w)

    Industry News: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct.
    • Recent findings suggest that it’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules.
    • Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.

    Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.

    In a recent development, “People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly crucial to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”.

    According to recent reports, the consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.

    “For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that manufacturer as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”.

    Recent findings suggest that plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he mentioned, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”.

    According to recent reports, of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a manufacturer like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.

    “I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the tech giant are almost impossible to separate,” he mentioned. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the tech giant.

    The Med Emre vessel capsized near Ibiza and Spain's Clara Campoamor, a pollution control vessel, was sent to assess the environmental impact.

    An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have noted.

    It has been revealed that the Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.

    The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.

    The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.

    "There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.

    Regional emergencies director Pablo GÃ¡rriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had been originally reported. The vessel remains, however, partially submerged.

    That made conditions more favourable for carrying out recovery operations, he said, "as we have gone from the possibility of the vessel being at a depth of 1,000m to a situation that allows operations to be carried out on the surface".

    According to recent reports, the Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.

    The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.

    According to recent reports, rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew remarked it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.

    The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.

    Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.

    In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline. It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

    #128361. Breaking: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming

    Breaking: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (735 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems.
    • A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material.
    • Industry observers note that because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don’t digest everything.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to newly introduced sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it.

    A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note.

    Industry observers note that because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don’t digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO2. That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane.

    Industry observers note that many peatlands have been drained by digging ditches that let water flow out to repurpose the land for agriculture or other uses. That lowers the water level, supplying oxygen to the exposed peat and ringing the aerobic bacteria dinner bell. Methane emissions get turned down, and CO2 emissions get turned way up.

    Recent findings suggest that the researchers used recent studies that measure gas emissions from peatlands to build a global model that estimated CO2 and methane release as the water level drops. The two gases respond differently to a given drop in water level, and CO2 in particular responds differently depending on where in the world the bog is located. Using reconstructions of water-level changes due to historical peatland drainage, the team ran their model starting in 1800.

    The simplest way to represent the climate impact of both CO2 and methane changes was to calculate the change in Earth’s energy budget—the strength of the greenhouse effect, in other words. They calculated the total effect in 2020 at about +83 milliwatts per square meter of the Earth’s surface from the CO2 emissions, and about -9 milliwatts per square meter from the reduced methane emissions, for a total effect of +73 mW. That is 2.7 percent of the total human-caused change in Earth’s energy budget. (With the error bars on all these numbers, it’s 1.8–3.6 percent.).

    Or to look at it another way, it means that around 4 percent of all the carbon that was buried in peatlands is now in the atmosphere.

    Regionally, over half of the total CO2 came from Europe, almost a quarter came from Southeast Asia, and only 14 percent came from North America. The timing is quite different, as well, with the contribution from Southeast Asia only jumping up in the last few decades.

    In a recent development, draining a peatland only starts the process of releasing carbon, though. So that means past land-use change will still be producing emissions in the future. To examine this, the researchers also ran their model forward to 2100.

    If peatland water levels were simply held constant from 2020 on, the total change in Earth’s energy budget would nearly double, from 73 to 138 milliwatts per square meter by 2100. Moderate restoration of peatland water levels could reduce that growth, and ambitious restoration could even cause the effect to shrink slightly below its 2020 potency in their analysis. This is a process we can halt if we really want to.

    But since rolling all the way back to the landscape of 1800 is unlikely, elevated emissions will continue for a long time. That makes this another part of the climate system where change plays out slowly, with long-term consequences.

    It has been revealed that nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11339-0 (About DOIs).

    • Twin sisters Romina (left) and Taraneh Rahimi were arrested in late January, their cousin says.
    • In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Twin sisters Romina (left) and Taraneh Rahimi were arrested in late January, their cousin says.

    Taraneh Rahimi is on death row in Iran.

    In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.

    She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.

    He claims Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.

    When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi claims, speaking from the US.

    He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.

    Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.

    In a recent development, the figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini indicates.

    January's protests began over economic grievances and spread to become Iran's largest since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

    The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".

    It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".

    It mentioned death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".

    The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.

    It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

    The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) claims it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.

    The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it indicates totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.

    In a recent development, the twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.

    Taraneh loves horses and would like to set up her own breeding centre one day, her cousin notes.

    Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which notes Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.

    Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.

    Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, claims both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".

    Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".

    According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.

    This image of Mahboubeh Shabani, sentenced to death in September, has been shared with human rights groups.

    Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.

    Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.

    She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.

    Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.

    "As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her claims.

    In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.

    The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it states is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.

    In a recent development, the woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing.".

    Najmeh Amini has been sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, rights groups say.

    Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".

    In a recent development, in response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".

    At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.

    She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".

    Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, claims "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".

    Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.

    However, Sato states as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".

    In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.

    Recent findings suggest that the death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned â though two of those have been sent for retrial. She states she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".

    Taraneh (left) and Romina both say they gave baseless confessions after being tortured.

    Sato indicates there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.

    According to recent reports, women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression.".

    The Iranian embassy noted judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh.".

    Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.

    Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.

    Nourmohammadi notes the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.

    Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he states.

    Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he indicates, and they tell her they initiative to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope.".

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    David Anthony Sanchez scammed victims out of $260,000 worth of cryptocurrency.

    A Florida man who is known as "Dave the Jewler" has been sentenced to 47 months in prison after running a cryptocurrency scam that involved using AI to impersonate a well-known streamer. David Anthony Sanchez, who pleaded guilty to money laundering and aggravated identity theft, was also ordered to pay restitution to the victims.

    As spotted by Aftermath, the US Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida mentioned Sanchez used AI to clone the voice of Mikyle "N3on" Rafiq in order to convince the people behind a memecoin project that the streamer had agreed to endorse, promote and take part in their scheme. The scammer pretended to be both N3on and the streamer's representative while communicating with the project's organizers.

    Sanchez fooled them into transferring around $260,000 worth of cryptocurrency to accounts he controlled. He then converted some of the crypto into US dollars that he used for his personal benefit.

    "Behind every fraud scheme are real people who suffer real financial harm," Yara Lorenzo Klukas, acting US Attorney for the Southern District of Florida, mentioned. "In this case, the defendant exploited artificial intelligence to manipulate the trust of unsuspecting victims and deprive them of their money. Today's sentence reflects our commitment to protecting victims, safeguarding the integrity of our financial markets and holding accountable those who exploit emerging technologies to defraud others.".

    It has been revealed that N3on's not exactly a stranger to AI clones of himself, as it happens. Aftermath noted that he tried using a deepfake of himself to keep his Kick stream going around the clock. N3on's likeness was also used in an AI-generated movie that was released a few months ago.

    FCC approves SpaceX blueprint to put AI data centers in space

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.
    • In a recent development, the FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences.
    • The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.

    In a recent development, the FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real strategy.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also stated the proposal “risks real harm.”.

    The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

    FCC Chair Brendan Carr remarked in a statement that the action “opens a bold upcoming frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”.

    Recent findings suggest that musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”.

    This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent.

    SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.

    In a recent development, the company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document.

    SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.

    Industry observers note that the FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

    #128349. Why GTA VI’s version of Florida feels so real

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1203 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 The Verge ↗ Open Full Page

    Why GTA VI’s version of Florida feels so real

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1203 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Virtual city expert Emma Fraser explains what makes Rockstar’s latest open world work.
    • There are plenty of reasons why Grand Theft Auto VI is so popular: the 13 years of anticipation, the relatable lead characters and romantic storyline, the sheer level of depth.
    • Industry observers note that “There’s something about this particular game that is really discombobulating and distracting in a sense,” she states.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Virtual city expert Emma Fraser explains what makes Rockstar’s latest open world work.

    There are plenty of reasons why Grand Theft Auto VI is so popular: the 13 years of anticipation, the relatable lead characters and romantic storyline, the sheer level of depth. But another major factor is the sense of place. The GTA series is unmatched when it comes to re-creating the feeling of a bustling, real-world city, and GTA VI’s fictional rendition of Florida is the studio’s most lifelike setting yet. It has functioning buses and trains, plentiful buildings you can go into and explore, residents you can chat with, and huge areas where you can interact with wildlife far away from the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City. For Emma Fraser, an assistant professor at UC Berkeley who studies urban ruins and virtual cities, the sense of realism has created a unique sensation while playing.

    Industry observers note that “There’s something about this particular game that is really discombobulating and distracting in a sense,” she states. “Because you have these moments where you think, ‘I’m in a place, I’m experiencing a location.’ You comprehend intellectually that it’s not real or that it’s at best a representation, but you still have this feeling in your brain and you’ll still dream about being in that place.”.

    Recent findings suggest that fraser teaches courses on topics including urban geography and virtual worlds and has written papers exploring topics like “mapping in the digital age” and “the virtual spectacle of the end of the city.” She says she started researching video game cities in part because, despite their influence and reach, they’re an underexplored space in academia. “I’m a geographer, and geographers are obsessed with cities,” she explains. “So much of geography is thinking about: How do we imagine cities? How do we navigate cities? How do we build cities? How do we map cities? And video games have all of that, but they’re not taken that seriously as an academic interest.”.

    Like much of the world, she’s been looking forward to GTA VI for years, particularly because of Rockstar’s on-the-ground approach to research. Before development on the game began, developers from the studio traveled to Florida to get an accurate picture. As GTA VI producer Rob Nelson told me, the starting point for the game was the setting, rather than the story or characters. “We just went around to feel it out,” he said. “Go to the Everglades, go to the Keys, go to the city, as many places as we can, and start thinking about what aspects of the place we want to incorporate.”.

    It has been revealed that while there are plenty of open-world games, many of the most successful — from Elden Ring to The Witcher — are sent in fantastical spaces. GTA stands apart in how its various settings look and feel true to the real world. And Fraser believes that this is one of the key reasons the series has such universal appeal. “You know immediately how to function in a city,” she explains. “You know there’s going to be law enforcement, there are going to be city blocks, there are going to be pedestrians, cars, and buses. It’s this really interesting environment that gives you a lot of possibilities to get a player more immersed in your world, because they already know a lot about a city as a general concept.”.

    “You can’t hold a whole city in your mind at one time.”.

    Recent findings suggest that fraser describes GTA VI’s world as having “implied expansiveness.” It’s not a one-to-one re-creation of the real location. There are plenty of things missing; you don’t see schools or daycares, and parking spaces are relatively sparse. But the game gets enough details right to be recognizable. Fraser explains that as long as certain parts of the city look correct — the lighting, the coastline, the decoration of street corners, the major arterial roads — that’s enough to convince people that they’re in something resembling Miami.

    It has been revealed that “You can’t hold a whole city in your mind at one time,” she indicates. “Instead it’s these highlights. What [Rockstar] do very successfully in the game is those snapshots. They’ve got far more content that is recognizable as Florida or Miami than they’ve been able to fit into previous games. So it’s a much more overwhelming sense of being in that place.” The “implied expansiveness” also comes in the form of dialogue, radio programs, and TV demonstrates that suggest a much bigger world by discussing places and moments that exist outside of the game you can actually explore.

    Sources indicate that this level of verisimilitude — combined with the fact that players can explore the city from multiple perspectives, everything from walking to flying a plane — has led to an experience that Fraser likens to virtual tourism, which can result in all kinds of different playstyles. “Some tourists are going to blow a lot of money on taxis and get to wherever they’re going as fast as they can,” she explains, “and some people just like sitting on a bus or a train and getting to know a place.” Similarly, there are certain players who will just experience the story and play through the main missions, and others who will get lost in side activities like bird watching.

    “Some people just like sitting on a bus or a train and getting to know a place”.

    What’s also notable about GTA VI is how its relationship-focused premise is motivating some players to experience the world in a much less violent way. And that includes how they move through the city. Some people are driving more carefully to avoid killing civilians, while others are exploring spaces while both characters hang out together. “In the first few games, you’re this empty vessel. You’re a criminal, you’re doing criminal things,” notes Fraser. “Whereas with GTA VI your motivation and the way you think about your character is really important.”.

    According to recent reports, now that the game is out and millions of players are venturing through Vice City, Fraser is hoping to use it to research the ways that real and virtual worlds intersect when it comes to how we navigate cities. GTA VI offers a lot of choice in this regard; you can still steal a Lambo and speed through the streets, but you can also hop on a train, put on some headphones, and listen to a podcast while getting where you need to be. “Because this world is so fully furnished, and you have so many options, you might start to import your own real-world practices into the game,” she says.

    In a recent development, but at this point, what has struck her most is the attention to detail that separates the universe of GTA VI from its contemporaries. “You can’t just generate a generic city and stick icons in, which is what a lot of games do,” she explains. “You aren’t going to get a sense of a real place if you do it that way.”.

    Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's LÃ©gion d'honneur in 1996.

    But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).

    Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.

    He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).

    Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.

    Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.

    Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".

    The appeal court remarked that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.

    Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation.".

    Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".

    French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.

    If you have been affected by any of the challenges raised in this story, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the firm’s management and governance practices.
    • Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P remarked in a statement.
    • The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the firm’s management and governance practices.

    Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P remarked in a statement.

    The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.

    Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.

    In August, Nvidia announced looks to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.

    A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Workers voted 75 percent against the IWGB recognition agreement.

    Workers voted 75 percent against the IWGB recognition agreement.

    Sources indicate that workers at Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games won’t unionize, after the vote for a formal recognition agreement failed, with only 25 percent of votes in favor of unionization. The Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) remarked that Rockstar workers in the union will continue organizing even without formal recognition.

    Voting ran from November 12th through 26th, covering the launch of GTA VI. If successful, the vote would have established a formal framework for collective negotiation with the studio over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, and pensions, along with a right to consultation over future changes including AI implementation and layoffs. Without it, Rockstar won’t have an obligation to meet union representatives, though workers and union members can still lobby for change informally.

    “For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society - this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for,” IWGB mentioned in a statement sent to The Verge. “Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.”.

    When Rockstar fired 31 IWGB members last year, the union accused it of “the most blatant and ruthless act of union busting in the history of the games industry.” That case has gone to a UK employment tribunal, with a judgment still pending.

    “We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI,” Rockstar head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe told Bloomberg News. “This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”.

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    As Anthropic IPOs, Grand Theft Auto VI proves why efficiency isn’t a virtue

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype.
    • GTA VI debuted as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ($2 billion).
    • The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It should have been impossible for “Grand Theft Auto VI” (GTA VI) to live up to the hype. Fans waited 13 years for the newest installment in the crime-adventure franchise, and Rockstar Games exceeded even those inconceivable expectations when the game finally came out last week.

    GTA VI debuted as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and made $3.79 billion on release day to mark what could be the biggest entertainment event ever – more massive than “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.9 billion) or Taylor Swift’s Eras tour ($2 billion).

    The 13-year wait certainly fueled the frenzy, and sales, around GTA VI, but some fans craved GTA VI because of what it represents in the emerging era of AI.

    Even the biggest workaholics among us – startup founders – scheduled time off to play the game, including Spiry co-founder Dima Beseda, who told TechCrunch, “I reshuffled my workload to free up time around the weekends and even booked vitamin IV drips to keep my energy up.”.

    Yet some players felt a sense of anticipatory nostalgia as they wiped away a layer of dust on their Xbox to play the game they’d been looking forward to since they were kids.

    “We do have a view that GTA is likely to be the last game of its kind to be made this way,” Ben Feder, managing partner at TIRTA Ventures and former CEO of Rockstar parent manufacturer Take-Two Interactive, told TechCrunch.

    That’s because GTA VI was created entirely without generative AI.

    According to recent reports, “We’re kind of at this technological moment where this way of developing has sort of reached its natural frontier,” Feder mentioned. “I don’t think you can say that games like this will always be around.”.

    Industry observers note that as millions of people immersed themselves in Vice City, the tech industry witnessed another long-awaited moment: Anthropic became the first major AI lab to go public. At Nasdaq HQ, Anthropic executives gathered to celebrate the Claude maker’s $81.3 billion IPO. At virtually the same moment that Anthropic broke the record for the largest IPO ever, GTA VI was also breaking records with the highest-rated and best-selling game launch of all time.

    But when the Anthropic team rang the bell on Thursday, the sound also signaled the end of an era in video game development, and perhaps even in the arts at large.

    According to recent reports, the AI industry operates with efficiency as its north star. The promise of this technology is that we will be able to automate so much work that we can expand the capabilities of humanity, avoiding needless time spent tinkering with ultimately fruitless ideas. Instead, a prompt goes into an LLM, and a response is spat out.

    This technological revolution exploded into the world with some soul-crushing side effects: children are inundated with mind-numbing slop on YouTube, lawyers cite nonexistent cases in court, and tech companies like Meta lay off tens of thousands of people as part of a corporate-branded “Year of Efficiency.” But against the backdrop of the AI industry’s first major IPO, Rockstar has unveiled a game that about 5,000 people labored over for more than a decade.

    Sources indicate that the final product is breathtaking, looking so lifelike that it can be hard to distinguish gameplay footage from real life. These sprawling open-world games are usually made possible by procedurally generating fresh landscapes and objects, but Rockstar has taken the time to painstakingly craft every detail of the world, even developing 30,000 different nonplayable characters with unique appearances and personalities.

    The video game industry is already grappling with the threat of AI. Google’s Project Genie, which released earlier this year, allows users to create and wander around 3D worlds generated from prompts to an LLM. The stock prices of several video game companies faltered around the time of Project Genie’s release, perhaps because of investors’ uncertainty about the future relevance of video game developers.

    It has been revealed that “The notion that somehow new tools would allow an individual to push a button and generate a hit, market a hit, and bring it to many millions of consumers around the world, it’s a laughable notion,” Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick mentioned at the time. “It’s just never been the case with entertainment.”.

    Recent findings suggest that zelnick’s fellow tech CEOs see different future, though. On a Meta earnings call this year, CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised that, “soon, you’ll have an AI that understands you and [can] even generate great personalized content for you.”.

    Elon Musk even went as far as proposing that a game like GTA VI could be made with AI.

    It has been revealed that “You won’t even have to ask,” Musk wrote on X. “AI will figure what video game you’d like best.”.

    This is the paradox of “Grandthropic” week. GTA VI is so impressively vast and captivating because its developers could make mistakes, experiment, and rework ideas, even if that meant delaying the game (twice). GTA VI was incubated with the exact inefficiencies that investors hope AI companies like Anthropic can help eradicate.

    According to recent reports, “Plenty of fantastic art — video games and elsewhere — almost by definition has to be created slowly, and there’s something to having that kind of inefficiency around it,” Feder noted. “Creative output requires deletion, right? Getting to kind of a masterpiece oftentimes requires an enormous amount of deletion. And when you’re talking about a game of the kind of complexity we’re talking about, that kind of deletion ends up being very expensive, and it is by definition not efficient.”.

    GTA VI reeks of its own humanity – every small detail is loaded with intention, but it’s this impressive precision that keeps the world abuzz, triggering the kind of monocultural moment that has become increasingly rare in a media landscape that revolves around highly personalized social media algorithms.

    The game forces the player to slow down, which is either frustrating or genius, depending on your sense of humor. People waited more than three presidential terms for the next installment in a high-octane action franchise, only to download a 212 GB behemoth of a game in which your earliest missions involve driving around doing errands and putting up drywall to make your girlfriend happy. Don’t worry — there are still car chases and shootouts — but in a moment when AI feels suffocating, GTA VI is such an artistic achievement that it is reaching audiences that don’t even like violent video games.

    The ultimate fantasy of GTA VI is no longer to role-play as a criminal — the fantasy is just taking your time to relish the mundane and explore an expansive world that developers were given the time and space to perfect.

    German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin Reuter.
    • A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.
    • Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin Reuter.

    A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

    Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.

    The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

    His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.

    We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He remarked he was reporting us to the police.

    According to recent reports, reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

    Sources indicate that the BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper SÃ¼ddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.

    Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.

    Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.

    A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled).

    At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.

    There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.

    In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

    There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that.".

    It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.

    French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is at the moment the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.

    The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.

    While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".

    Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.

    In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.

    In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.

    Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.

    News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.

    According to recent reports, he was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.

    One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cans.

    The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

    The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.

    Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.

    The men claimed they had been paid up to â¬1,000-a-time (Â£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.

    "Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is mentioned to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye.".

    Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boats.

    Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.

    Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.

    Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.

    On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.

    The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.

    Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German police.

    Meanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.

    Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.

    The MaReBoote firm address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.

    Industry observers note that we confronted Marvin Reuter at his manufacturer premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rules.

    When we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.

    Industry observers note that he then returned a short time later and stated he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.

    We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.

    It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.

    Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near Dortmund.

    In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.

    The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the fresh law had been used.

    Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

    The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an key piece of the puzzle".

    While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.

    The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

    The Hidden Problems Behind Website-to-CRM Integrations (and How to Prevent Them)

    📅 31 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
    • Industry observers note that connecting a website form to a customer relationship management (CRM) system may seem straightforward.
    • It has been revealed that the integration may work perfectly during the first test.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
